headline: Connecticut directs $15 million to expand after-school programs across the state
dek: The three-year federal grant package will support 25 programs serving schools in communities including Bridgeport, Hartford, New Haven, Stamford and Waterbury, with another 11 recipients planned for 2027–28.
body: Connecticut is committing about $15 million over three years to expand after-school learning, mentoring and enrichment programs, the state Department of Education announced Oct. 7. The federal 21st Century Community Learning Center awards will fund 25 programs beginning Oct. 1, 2026, and are aimed at students in schools with high concentrations of low-income students. The first-year awards total $4,905,155, according to the department’s published recipient table.

The grants reach a broad group of school districts and community organizations. Current-year recipients include programs in Bridgeport, Bristol, East Hartford, Hartford, Hamden, Killingly, Manchester, Meriden, Middletown, New London, Norwalk, Stamford, Torrington and Waterbury. Awards range from $94,349 for a Carver program serving Side by Side Charter School in Norwalk to $227,500 for several projects, including programs in Bridgeport, Hamden and Waterbury. The state received 55 applications and says the awards were selected through a competitive review.

The money is designed to extend the school day rather than simply provide child care. The [U.S. Department of Education’s program description](https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/formula-grants/school-improvement-grants/nita-m-lowey-21st-century-community-learning-centers-title-iv-part-b) says 21st Century Community Learning Centers support academic enrichment in reading, math and other subjects, along with broader activities and family educational services during non-school hours. Connecticut’s announcement lists tutoring, science and technology, mentoring, arts, athletics, wellness, cultural programs and family engagement among the possible uses.

The local structure matters because the grant does not create one statewide after-school schedule. Districts and nonprofit lead applicants will operate the programs, identify participating students and decide how to fit activities around their school communities. In Torrington, for example, [EdAdvance says its BASES program uses 21st CCLC funding](https://bases.edadvance.org/grantsandpartners) for sites at Torrington Intermediate School and Torrington Middle School. That kind of school-by-school arrangement means families will need to look to their district or provider for enrollment rules, hours, transportation and the exact services available.

The department is also reserving roughly $2.1 million for 11 additional recipients in a three-year cohort scheduled to begin in the 2027–28 school year. Those planned awards include programs connected to schools in Bristol, East Hartford, Groton, Middletown, New Haven and Waterbury. The future cohort is separate from the 25 programs starting this fall, and the department says both federal funding and compliance with program requirements must continue for the awards to remain in place.

The federal grants are part of a larger Connecticut after-school investment. The state says it is separately providing about $5.3 million for 41 programs during the 2026–27 school year, bringing the combined annual state and federal investment to about $10 million. Those figures describe funding streams, not the number of children served. The Oct. 7 release does not provide a statewide enrollment total, a common attendance target or a single measure that will show whether the new programs improve academic outcomes.

That unanswered implementation question will shape the program’s regional impact. The awards put new resources into communities where schools and families may need supervised time, academic support and enrichment beyond regular hours, but the value will depend on staffing, participation and continuity. The immediate change is that local organizations have funding authority and named school sites; the next step is for them to publish schedules and turn the grants into programs families can actually use.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut awards $15 million for after-school programs
seoDescription: Connecticut announced $15 million in three-year 21st Century Community Learning Center awards for 25 after-school programs, with another 11 planned for 2027–28.
